public_rationale: The UK National Audit Office investigated WannaCry's impact on the NHS. It concluded the attack was relatively unsophisticated and could have been prevented by basic IT security best practice. NHS Digital told the NAO that every infected organisation shared the same vulnerability, unpatched or unsupported Windows, and could have taken relatively simple action to protect itself, such as patching or managing firewalls. Patch alerts had gone out in March and April 2017. This matches Marcus's claim. One caveat: the NAO also blamed the Department of Health's weak oversight, so responsibility was not only the hospitals'.
limitations: The NAO covered NHS England only, and infected organisations included GP practices as well as hospitals.
The NAO is reporting NHS Digital's view on the shared vulnerability.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: WannaCry's damage to hospitals could have been largely avoided if the hospitals had kept up with cybersecurity procedures.
conditions: if hospitals had kept up on cybersecurity procedures

statement.excerpt: The whole WannaCry fiasco could have been largely avoided if hospitals had kept up on cybersecurity procedures.

from_speaker: if hospitals had kept up on cybersecurity procedures
our_interpretation: Read as the claim that the 2017 WannaCry damage to the NHS was largely preventable through basic security practice by affected NHS organisations, such as patching and firewall management.
'Hospitals' is read as the NHS trusts and other NHS organisations hit by the attack.
criteria.support_condition: An official review finds the WannaCry infections in the NHS could have been prevented by basic IT security practice, such as applying available patches or managing firewalls.
criteria.contradiction_condition: An official review finds the infections could not reasonably have been prevented by local security practice, for example because no fix was available or the attack was highly sophisticated.

evidence.excerpt: It was a relatively unsophisticated attack and could have been prevented by the NHS following basic IT security best practice.
evidence.locator: quote from Amyas Morse, head of the NAO
evidence.explanation: The head of the UK public spending auditor says the attack was preventable through basic IT security practice, which matches Marcus's claim.

evidence.excerpt: all organisations infected by WannaCry shared the same vulnerability and could have taken relatively simple action to protect themselves. Infected organisations had unpatched, or unsupported Windows operating systems so were susceptible to the ransomware.
evidence.explanation: Ties the infections to local failures to patch or manage firewalls, which is the 'keeping up on cybersecurity procedures' Marcus describes.

evidence.excerpt: In March and April 2017, NHS Digital had issued critical alerts warning organisations to patch their systems to prevent WannaCry. However, before 12 May 2017, the Department had no formal mechanism for assessing whether local NHS organisations had complied
evidence.explanation: Confirms patch alerts were issued before the attack. It also shows the NAO placed some blame on central oversight, not only on local hospitals.
